reference.source: Hand surgery and sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Injury to the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint, causing pain and instability with pinch and grip
The acute form (skier's thumb) follows forced abduction of the thumb, classically a fall onto an outstretched hand holding a ski pole
The chronic form (the original gamekeeper's thumb) results from repetitive stress
A Stener lesion, in which the torn ligament end is displaced superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, prevents healing and needs surgery
Careful stress testing assesses instability, ideally after excluding an associated avulsion fracture on radiographs
Partial injuries are treated with immobilisation, whereas complete tears and Stener lesions require surgical repair
reference.pathophysiology: Gamekeeper's thumb involves disruption of the ulnar collateral ligament that stabilises the thumb metacarpophalangeal joint against valgus (radially directed) stress during pinch. Acute forced radial deviation tears the ligament, usually at its distal insertion, sometimes with a bony avulsion. If the ligament fully ruptures, its proximal-to-distal recoil can leave the torn end trapped superficial to the adductor aponeurosis (a Stener lesion), which physically blocks healing. Loss of ligament integrity produces instability that impairs pinch strength and, if untreated, leads to chronic instability and arthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Radial collateral ligament injury of the thumb
First carpometacarpal joint injury or osteoarthritis
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs to identify an avulsion fracture before stress testing
Stress testing of the metacarpophalangeal joint in extension and slight flexion
Ultrasound or MRI to detect a Stener lesion or complete tear
Assessment of pinch stability and strength
redFlags: Gross instability indicating a complete tear
reference.prognosis: Partial injuries generally recover well with immobilisation, and surgically repaired complete tears or Stener lesions usually regain good stability and pinch, whereas missed injuries can cause chronic instability and secondary arthritis.
pitfalls: Missing a Stener lesion, which will not heal without surgery
Performing vigorous stress testing before excluding an avulsion fracture
Undertreating a complete tear as a simple sprain
Overlooking chronic instability as a source of ongoing weakness
management: Immobilisation in a thumb spica cast or splint for partial, incomplete ulnar collateral ligament injuries
Surgical repair, or reattachment of a bony avulsion, for complete tears and for a Stener lesion, which cannot heal without operation
Radiographs before stress testing to identify an associated avulsion fracture
Analgesia and initial protection of the metacarpophalangeal joint
Hand therapy and graded rehabilitation to restore pinch strength and stability after immobilisation or repair
Referral to hand surgery for complete tears, Stener lesions or chronic instability
